definition: A fuzzy control system is a control system based on fuzzy logic – a mathematical system that analyzes analog input values in terms of logical variables that take on continuous values between 0 and 1, in contrast to classical or digital logic, which operates on discrete values of either 1 or 0 (true or false, respectively).
details: Fuzzy logic is widely used in machine control. The term "fuzzy" refers to the fact that the logic involved can deal with concepts that cannot be expressed as the "true" or "false" but rather as "partially true". Although alternative approaches such as genetic algorithms and neural networks can perform just as well as fuzzy logic in many cases, fuzzy logic has the advantage that the solution to the problem can be cast in terms that human operators can understand, such that that their experience can be used in the design of the controller. This makes it easier to mechanize tasks that are already successfully performed by humans.

explainer.lead: A fuzzy control system steers a machine using degrees of truth, so an input can be partly true rather than simply yes or no. It is useful in machine control because human operators can express their experience in understandable terms and use it to design the controller.

tiers.eli5: Imagine describing a room as “a little warm” instead of choosing only “hot” or “not hot.” A fuzzy controller can use that in-between description to decide how a machine should respond. This helps it copy tasks that people already know how to do.
tiers.practitioner: Fuzzy control is applied in machine control by converting analog inputs into continuous truth values and designing the controller around human-readable operating knowledge. Its main practical advantage is that operators can understand the solution and contribute their experience. It is not automatically superior: genetic algorithms and neural networks can perform just as well in many cases.
tiers.paperLevel: A fuzzy control system is a controller based on fuzzy logic, in which an analog input is described by logical variables with values μ(x) ∈ [0, 1], rather than classical values in {0, 1}. Intermediate values represent partial truth. The approach supports human-interpretable controller design, although alternative methods such as neural networks and genetic algorithms can perform equally well in many cases.

explainer.example: For a heater, a temperature input need not be classified only as “warm” or “not warm.” It can be assigned an intermediate degree of warmth, such as 0.6, allowing the fuzzy controller to base its response on the room being partly warm rather than switching between two absolute descriptions.

usedIn.name: Machine control
usedIn.detail: Fuzzy logic is widely used to control machines through inputs that can express partial truth.

usedIn.name: Human-operated task automation
usedIn.detail: Operators’ experience can be incorporated into controllers for tasks already performed successfully by people.

explainer.intuition: Real-world descriptions often sit between completely true and completely false. Fuzzy control uses that middle ground directly instead of forcing every analog input into a binary decision.
howItWorks: Read an analog input from the machine or its environment.
Describe the input using logical variables whose values range continuously from 0 to 1.
Interpret intermediate values as degrees of partial truth.
Use the fuzzy-logic controller, informed where useful by human operating experience, to determine the machine’s control response.
explainer.whyItMatters: It makes analog machine control compatible with concepts people naturally express as partly true. Because the resulting solution can remain understandable to human operators, their experience can help shape the controller.
misconceptions: “Fuzzy” does not mean random or imprecise; it means that truth values can be continuous between 0 and 1.
Fuzzy control is not always better than neural networks or genetic algorithms, which can perform just as well in many cases.
